summary: One of two FYI Questions and Answers documents from the IETF User Services Working Group, collecting answers to commonly asked new Internet user questions. It was replaced by RFC 1594.

eli5.summary: A help sheet for newcomers. It lists questions people often asked when they first got on the Internet, and gives simple answers.

questions: fyi questions and answers new users
subtitle: A guide for new Internet users answering frequently asked questions

tldr.problem: New Internet users need practical answers to common questions about how the Internet works, what it offers, and how to use its services.
tldr.mechanism: This FYI document systematically answers questions about the Internet, TCP/IP protocols, the Domain Name System, Internet standards and documentation, major organizations, available services, and related terminology.
tldr.outcome: The document was later updated and superseded by RFC 1594, but it remains a useful reference for understanding how the early Internet was explained to newcomers in 1992.

today: RFC 1325 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 1594. It is Historic as a document series, though the protocols and services it describes have evolved significantly since its 1992 publication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This FYI document is designed for new Internet users joining the community and discovering what the Internet offers. It addresses the most commonly asked questions about the network, its protocols, services, and organizations. Rather than having the same questions asked repeatedly on mailing lists, this document provides centralized answers that the Internet community can reference.

The document is maintained by the User Services Working Group of the IETF. As new questions emerge and answers need updating, new versions of this FYI are published, always retaining the designation FYI 4 to help users locate the current version.
sections.eli5: This document answers the questions that newcomers always ask about the Internet, so people don't have to keep answering the same things over and over.

sections.title: What Is the Internet and What Can You Do?
sections.content:
The Internet is a large collection of networks, all running TCP/IP protocols, interconnected so that users on any network can reach users on any other. It grew from the ARPANET and now includes networks at universities, research institutions, government facilities, and corporations. The key distinction is that the Internet specifically refers to TCP/IP-based networks, though other networks like BITNET and DECnet can exchange mail with the Internet through gateways.

New users have many capabilities once connected: they can move files between hosts using file transfer, establish remote connections to other computers, send electronic mail across the Internet and to many non-Internet networks, and access specialized databases and information archives. The Internet Resource Guide, published by the NSF Network Service Center, lists publicly accessible resources including supercomputer centers, library catalogs, and specialized data collections.
sections.eli5: The Internet is computers everywhere connected together so you can share files, send mail, and talk to computers far away. Once you're on it, you can do lots of things like send email, copy files, or look up information.

sections.title: Internet Standards and Documentation
sections.content:
Request for Comments (RFCs) are working notes of the Internet research community. They cover topics from network protocol specifications to policy studies to workshop summaries. RFCs receive technical review but are not formally refereed. Anyone can submit a document for publication as an RFC by sending it to the RFC Editor. RFCs are never revised once published; instead, a protocol can be improved and re-documented in multiple separate RFCs. Once published, an RFC keeps its number forever, so there is never ambiguity about whether you have the most recent version of a particular RFC.

FYI (For Your Information) documents are a subset of RFCs designed to provide users with information about Internet topics. They are more information-oriented than the typically technical RFCs. Each FYI gets both an FYI number and an RFC number; the FYI number stays the same even if the document is updated with a new RFC number, making it easy to identify FYI documents by topic.

STD (Standards) numbers identify RFCs that document Internet standards. An STD number is assigned only to specifications that complete the standardization process. Like FYI numbers, an STD number remains constant even if the standard is re-specified with a new RFC number.
sections.eli5: The Internet has three ways to publish important documents. RFCs are the working notes of people building the Internet. FYIs are like help guides for users. STDs mark the official standards. Each keeps its number so you can always find the latest version.

sections.title: The Internet's Governing Bodies
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering, and management. It sets Internet standards, manages the RFC publication process, reviews the IETF and IRTF, performs strategic planning, acts as an international technical liaison, and resolves issues that neither the IETF nor IRTF can handle.

The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is a large open community of network designers, operators, vendors, and researchers who coordinate Internet operation and evolution. The IETF is organized around technical areas, each managed by a director, and meets three times a year. It is the primary source of proposed protocol standards submitted to the IAB.

The Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) promotes research in networking and development of new technology. While there is overlap with the IETF, the IRTF focuses on longer-term research directions.

The Internet Society is a professional non-profit organization fostering the Internet's well-being and evolution. It works to educate the public about Internet technology, promote educational applications, and provide a forum for collaboration.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) coordinates assignment of protocol parameter values such as operation codes, type fields, and object identifiers, ensuring no conflicts in Internet protocol implementations. Internet addresses and Autonomous System numbers are assigned by the DDN NIC, which serves as the Internet Registry.
sections.eli5: Several organizations work together to run the Internet. The IAB decides on big-picture rules. The IETF discusses protocols and solutions to problems. The IRTF does research. The Internet Society promotes the Internet. The IANA keeps track of special numbers so everyone doesn't use the same ones.

sections.title: Internet Services and Tools
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) translates human-readable hostnames into network addresses. It uses a hierarchical, distributed structure that eliminates the need for a centrally maintained file mapping all host names to addresses. A Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) includes all domain labels from a specific host up to the root, such as PARIS.NISC.SRI.COM.

Electronic mail is addressed in the form user@domain and can reach users on many networks beyond the Internet itself. Mailing lists are aliases with multiple destinations, usually created to discuss specific topics, with administrative requests typically sent to listname-request addresses.

Anonymous FTP allows users to sign on to a remote computer and copy public files. Users log in with username "anonymous" and often use their email address as the password.

TELNET is the remote login protocol allowing interactive connections to remote computers. The term is used both as the protocol name and as a verb meaning to establish a remote connection.

USENET (Netnews) is a distributed information service handling news, not mail, using various underlying networks for transport. Unlike the Internet, it is not centrally administered.

Archie is a system for automatically tracking anonymous FTP archive sites, developed by McGill University. It makes available the names and locations of millions of files at hundreds of archive sites and can be accessed via TELNET, email, or client programs.
sections.eli5: The Internet offers several tools: DNS finds computers by name, email sends messages, FTP copies files, TELNET connects remotely, USENET is like a bulletin board, and archie helps you find files stored on computers.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1325 is an Informational document, meaning it provides information to the Internet community without specifying a standard. Published in May 1992, it was part of the User Services Working Group's effort to document knowledge for an expanding Internet community.

This document obsoletes RFC 1206, its predecessor, and is itself obsoleted by RFC 1594, a more recent version. While superseded, RFC 1325 remains a snapshot of how the Internet was explained to newcomers at a pivotal moment in the network's growth, when it was transitioning from research infrastructure to broader adoption.
sections.eli5: This document was an official guide from 1992 that was later replaced by a newer version. It shows what the Internet was like back then and the kinds of questions new users had.
